name: Nyore
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Kanyoro, Rachel A. 1983. Unity in Diversity: A Linguistic Survey of the Abaluyia of Western Kenya (covers Nyore phonology; not online)
earlier_scan.note: Luyia survey plausibly covers Nyore prosody; no online copy found

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2013. Verb tone in Bantu languages: micro-typological patterns and research methods. Africana Linguistica 19: 137-234.
sources.note: Grepped: no Kenyan Nyore (JE33) data or statement.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x langdoc list for nyor1244 (6 refs: Kanyoro 1983, Schoenbrun 1994/1997, Ochilo 2018, ISO 2007, Kweya 2011) and OLAC listing for nyd (Wayback 2024: Bible portion, Crúbadán, Ethnologue, Van Otterloo 1979 SIL intelligibility testing).
sources.note: No grammar, sketch or phonology of Kenyan Nyore is registered anywhere; confirms the description gap.

sources.citation: Kisembe, Evelyne. 2005. A linguistic analysis of Luyia varieties spoken in western Kenya. MA thesis, Memorial University of Newfoundland, 110 pp. hdl:20.500.14783/12907
sources.note: Historical segmental processes (Bantu Spirantization, Dahl's Law, Luyia Law) in 12 varieties; Nyore not among them; no prosody.

sources.citation: Asungu, Kwendo & Emily Ayieta Ondondo. 2024. An analysis of phonological nativisation of English loanwords in Olunyole: an Optimality Theoretic approach. IJRISS 8(10): 882-894. doi:10.47772/IJRISS.2024.8100072
sources.note: Olunyole segment substitution and open-syllable structure (CV, V, CVV; no codas, simple onsets); no discussion of tone or stress at all.

sources.citation: Asungu, Kwendo, Emily Ayieta Ondondo & Robert Ochieng. 2024. Morphological nativization of English loanwords in Olunyole: a constraints-based analysis. JEREDA 5(2): 194-208. doi:10.47434/JEREDA.5.2.2024.194
sources.note: Noun-class assignment of loans; nothing on prosody.

sources.citation: Anindo, Violet. 2021. Fonolojia ya maneno mkopo ya Kinyore kutoka Kiswahili. MA thesis (Kiswahili), University of Nairobi, 110 pp. hdl:11295/160343
sources.note: In Swahili. Segment inventory, vowel length contrast, syllable structure of Kinyore; p.87: 'Kinyore kina toni. Huu utafiti wetu haukushughulikia toni.' (Kinyore has tone; this study did not treat tone). Nothing on stress (mkazo appears only in a reproduced Kiparsky lexical-phonology diagram).

sources.citation: Osotsi, Eric Mbeya. 2020. A systematic reconstruction of the phonology of Proto-Luyia: a comparative analysis. MA project, University of Nairobi, 127 pp. hdl:11295/154048
sources.note: Comparative segmental reconstruction across Luyia varieties incl. Nyore; tone/length excluded; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Ochilo, George Ogot. 2018. The effect of Dholuo on Lunyore: a case of lexical borrowing. MA project, University of Nairobi, 103 pp. hdl:11295/105534
sources.note: Lexical/sociolinguistic; no phonology chapter; nothing on stress or tone.

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R., Minah Nabirye, Deo Kawalya & Gilles-Maurice de Schryver. 2017. A sketch of Lower Nyole tone. Africana Linguistica 23: 215ff.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: online with a university library login (also: harvard online access (harvardkey))
sources.note: About Ugandan (Lower) Nyole JE35, NOT Kenyan Nyore; fn.1 explicitly warns the two are confused in the literature (Mould 1981 and Angogo Kanyoro 1983 discuss Kenyan Nyore). Not usable for nyor1244.

sources.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J., Christopher R. Green & Michael R. Marlo. 2014. Luyia tone melodies. Africana Linguistica 20: 121-143.
sources.note: Idakho, Wanga etc.; Nyore not covered; 'penult' occurs only as a tonal target position; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2009. Luyia tonal dialectology. Talk handout, Dept. of Linguistics and Languages, University of Nairobi, 16 Dec 2009 (Wayback copy).
sources.note: Bibliographic survey (3): the only tone reference listed for Nyore is 'Key & Bosire 2003'; Nyore dictionary materials 'remain hand-written'. No Nyore data; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Key, Michael Parrish & Mokaya Bosire. 2004 [presented WOCAL 4 / ACAL 34, Rutgers, June 2003]. Leftward High tone spread and downstep in Nyore. Rutgers Optimality Archive ROA-644, 15 pp. https://roa.rutgers.edu/files/644-0204/
sources.note: First-hand sketch of Nyore (E.33) verbal tonology from a native speaker: verb roots H-toned vs toneless, 'only a H vs. Ø tonal contrast', leftward binary H spread of prefixal Hs, downstep vs fusion across the macrostem boundary. The words stress/accent/penultimate never occur; no statement on word stress. Fn.1: 'We are unaware of any prior linguistic or tonal description of Nyore.'

sources.citation: Kanyoro, Rachel Msimbi Angogo. 1983. Unity in diversity: a linguistic survey of the Abaluyia of western Kenya (Beiträge zur Afrikanistik, Bd. 20; Veröffentlichungen der Institute für Afrikanistik und Ägyptologie der Universität Wien). Wien: Afro-Pub. 322 pp.

sources.note: The only published linguistic survey covering all 17 Kenyan Luyia dialects including Nyore, with comparative phonology chapters; the earlier world scan named it as the likely place for a Nyore prosody remark (tone/stress) and Marlo et al. 2017 confirm it discusses Kenyan Nyore.

sources.citation: Malanda, Mukuna Stephen. 2005. A synchronic study of the major phonological processes of the Lunyore and Lutachoni dialects of Luyia consonantal systems. MA thesis, University of Nairobi. hdl:11295/18678

sources.note: Only Nairobi thesis devoted to Lunyore phonology proper; background chapter may characterize suprasegmentals (tone/stress) even though the focus is consonantal.
